items.title: Postgres as a job queue
items.summary: How SKIP LOCKED lets several workers take jobs from one table without taking the same job twice.
key_points: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED skips the rows that others hold
A lease and a reaper give back the jobs of a dead worker
Handlers must be idempotent: a job can run two times
items.text:
A job queue needs three things: a place to keep the jobs, a way for a worker to take one job that no other worker takes, and a way to give a job back when its worker dies.

Postgres can do all three with one table. Each job is a row with a state. A worker takes the next job with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED: the rows that another transaction holds are skipped, not waited for. So ten workers can poll the same table, and each one gets a different row.

The lock alone is not enough. If the worker holds the row lock for the whole job, a long job keeps a transaction open for minutes. Better: take the job in a short transaction, write a lease (the name of the worker and a time until which the job is its own), and commit. The work happens outside any transaction.

A reaper finds the jobs whose lease ended and makes them ready again. This means a job can run two times: once by the worker that was too slow, and once by the next one. So each handler must be idempotent: running it again must not do the work two times.

Retries need a backoff. A job that fails waits longer each time, and after a limit it becomes dead, so that a person can look at it.

The advantage over a separate broker is the transaction. The job is written in the same transaction as the data that it is about, so a job never points at data that was rolled back.

Watch the table itself. Finished jobs pile up, and each update of a state leaves a dead row version behind. Delete or archive finished jobs on a schedule, and keep an index on the columns that the next query reads: the state and the time after which the job may run.

A queue in the database has limits. Each poll is a query, so a thousand workers polling every second is a thousand queries each second. LISTEN and NOTIFY can wake the workers instead of a short poll interval. And when the jobs are many millions each day, a dedicated broker is the better tool; below that, one table is simpler to run and to debug.

items.title: How MVCC keeps old row versions
items.summary: Why an update writes a new version of a row, what a snapshot sees, and why VACUUM exists.
key_points: A long transaction keeps old versions alive
VACUUM removes the versions that nobody can see
items.text:
Postgres never changes a row in place. An UPDATE writes a new version of the row and marks the old one as dead for the transactions that start later. A DELETE only marks the row.

Each transaction sees a snapshot: the versions that were committed when it started. A long transaction therefore keeps old versions alive, because it can still need them.

VACUUM removes the versions that no transaction can see any more. Autovacuum runs it in the background, when a table has enough dead rows. A table that is updated often and never vacuumed grows: this is called bloat.

The same design explains why a long open transaction is dangerous in production. It does not only hold its locks. It also stops VACUUM from cleaning up after everybody else, and the tables grow while it is open.

Transaction ids are 32 bits. Postgres freezes old rows so that the counter can wrap around safely; this is the other job of VACUUM. If VACUUM falls behind for a very long time, Postgres stops accepting writes to protect the data: the transaction id wraparound.

Indexes have the same problem as tables. An index entry can point at a dead row version, and a scan must visit the table to check whether the row is visible. A visibility map marks the pages where all rows are visible, so that an index-only scan can skip the table for them.

Good habits follow from this. Keep transactions short. Do not leave a session idle inside a transaction. Watch the oldest transaction in pg_stat_activity, and the number of dead rows in pg_stat_user_tables.

items.title: HNSW indexes in pgvector
items.summary: An approximate nearest neighbour index: how its graph works, what ef_search does, and why filters are a trap.
key_points: A WHERE clause is applied after the index scan
Measure recall against an exact search first
items.text:
An exact nearest neighbour search compares the query vector with every vector. For a few hundred thousand vectors this is fine. For millions it is slow, and an approximate index helps.

HNSW builds a graph in layers. The top layer has few nodes and long links; each lower layer has more nodes and shorter links. A search starts at the top and walks down, always towards the closest node. It finds most of the true nearest neighbours, not all of them: that is the trade-off.

The parameter ef_search sets how many candidates the search keeps. A larger value finds more of the true neighbours and is slower. With the default of 40, a query returns at most 40 rows.

Filtering is the trap. With an approximate index, the WHERE clause is applied after the index scan. If the filter keeps one row in ten, a scan of 40 candidates leaves about four. pgvector 0.8 added iterative scans, which go on scanning until enough rows pass the filter.

Before adding an index, measure: recall against an exact search, and latency.

An HNSW index is built in memory, so the build is fast only when maintenance_work_mem is large enough for the graph. It also grows the table on disk: each vector appears in the graph with its links.

The other index type of pgvector, IVFFlat, cuts the space into lists around centroids, and a search reads the closest lists. It builds faster and needs less memory, but its quality depends on the data that existed when it was built: train it after the table has its data, and build it again when the data changes a lot.

items.title: How to cut documents into pieces for retrieval
items.summary: The size of a piece, where to cut it, and why overlap has a cost.
key_points: Cut after a paragraph or a sentence
Keep the position of each piece
items.text:
A retrieval system rarely searches whole documents. A long page about many things gets one vector that is about nothing in particular. So documents are cut into pieces, and each piece gets its own vector.

The size of a piece is a trade-off. A small piece is precise but loses its context: a sentence like "it is faster" means nothing alone. A large piece keeps the context but mixes topics.

Good cuts follow the structure of the text: a paragraph, a section, a list. When a paragraph is too long, cut after a sentence. Only a word that is longer than a whole piece is cut inside.

Some systems let pieces overlap, so that a sentence at a border appears in both pieces. Overlap costs storage and makes duplicates in the results; a search must then join them by document.

Keep the position of each piece in the original text. Then a result can show the passage and link to the exact place in the document.

Measure the effect of each choice with a golden set of questions. A change of the piece size can move recall by many points, in either direction, and intuition is a poor guide. Also check the number of pieces per document: a very long book can make thousands of pieces, and a search then returns many pieces of the same book.

items.title: LoRA: fine-tuning with low-rank adapters
items.summary: Fine-tuning a large model by training two thin matrices instead of all the weights.
key_points: The original weights stay frozen
QLoRA keeps them in 4 bits
items.text:
Fine-tuning all the weights of a large language model needs as much memory as training it. LoRA avoids this. It freezes the original weights and learns a small update for some matrices: the product of two thin matrices, of rank 8 or 16.

Only these small matrices are trained, so the optimizer state is tiny, and one GPU can tune a model that it could not train. After training, the update can be added into the weights, so the model runs at the same speed as before.

QLoRA goes further: it keeps the frozen weights in 4 bits. The quality stays close to a full fine-tune on many tasks.

The rank is the main knob. A higher rank can learn more, and it needs more memory. For a narrow task, such as a fixed output format, a small rank is often enough.

items.title: Attention, step by step
items.summary: Queries, keys and values, the softmax over the scores, and why the cost grows with the square of the length.
key_points: Each head can follow a different relation
Long contexts need caching or windows
items.text:
Attention lets each token look at the other tokens and decide which ones matter for it. Each token makes three vectors: a query, a key and a value. The score of a pair is the dot product of the query of one token and the key of the other, divided by the square root of the size.

A softmax turns the scores into weights, and the output of a token is the weighted sum of the values. Multi-head attention does this several times in parallel with smaller vectors: each head can follow a different relation, such as the previous word or the subject of the verb.

The cost grows with the square of the length of the text, because every pair is scored. Long contexts therefore need tricks: caching the keys and values of earlier tokens, or attention that only looks at a window.

items.title: The transactional outbox pattern
items.summary: Publishing an event and changing the data in one transaction, with a relay that sends the event later.
key_points: The event goes into an outbox table
Consumers must handle duplicates
items.text:
A service writes to its database and must also publish an event. If it writes first and publishes second, a crash between the two loses the event. If it publishes first, a crash can publish an event about data that was never committed.

The transactional outbox solves this. The service writes the event into an outbox table, in the same transaction as the data. A separate relay reads the outbox and publishes the events, then marks them as sent.

The relay can publish an event two times, for example when it crashes after publishing and before marking. So consumers must handle duplicates: each event has an id, and a consumer remembers the ids that it has seen.

The pattern turns two writes into one atomic write plus a retry loop. It is the same idea as a job queue in the same database: the work is recorded in the transaction that makes it necessary.

The relay can be a polling loop over the outbox table, or a reader of the write-ahead log of the database (change data capture). Polling is simple and adds load; reading the log adds no queries but needs another moving part.

Keep the outbox small: delete the events after they are sent, or partition the table by day and drop old partitions.

items.title: Leases and fencing tokens
items.summary: Why a lock with a timeout is not safe alone, and how a fencing token makes it safe.
key_points: A paused client can outlive its lease
The storage refuses an old token
items.text:
A distributed lock with a timeout is a lease: a client holds it until a moment, and then it expires. Leases are safe only if a client that lost its lease cannot do harm.

The classic failure: a client takes the lease, then pauses for a long garbage collection. The lease expires, a second client takes it and writes. The first client wakes up, still believes that it holds the lease, and writes too.

A fencing token prevents this. Each new lease gets a larger number. The storage remembers the largest token that it has seen, and it refuses a write with a smaller one. So the paused client is fenced out, even though it does not know that its lease ended.

The token must be checked by the resource itself. A check by the client is not enough, because the client is the part that can be wrong.

Clocks make it worse. A lease is measured in time, and the clocks of two machines drift. A client must stop well before its lease ends, with a margin for drift and for the pause of a garbage collection.

The same pattern appears in leader election. A new leader gets a larger term number, and the followers refuse messages of an older term.
